extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature/philosophy interested in moral, political, and military reflection (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative observations and practical principles from Montaigne's essays about leadership, military conduct, moderation, and marriage — informal criteria for judging character and strategy. The text offers anecdotal examples and judgments (e.g., about Caesar, generals, soldiers, and exemplary women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clemency and leniency as political/military policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar left captured captains at liberty, proclaimed as friends those who did not take up arms against him, and left conquered cities free to choose sides, imposing no garrison but the memory of his gentleness and clemency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: setting prisoners at liberty; sparing citizens on the day of Pharsalia; answering insults gently and later advancing enemies (making them consul). Caveat: Montaigne judges such proceedings 'very hazardous' and attributes their success to Caesar's unique fortune and foresight — they may not generalize to other actors or contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and care for friends as a mark of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar showed respect for friends (e.g., leaving his only lodging to Caius Oppius and sleeping on the ground), and manifested moderation in victory and resolution in adversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative acts include personal sacrifice for friends and adherence to justice (even executing a beloved servant for wrongdoing). These behaviors exemplify moderation and personal honour in triumphant and adverse circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition as a corrupting rudder
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive ambition can spoil noble qualities: Caesar's clemency, liberality, and other virtues were 'stifled and spoiled by his furious ambition' which made him 'a public thief' and led to vanity, seeking divine honours, and erecting glory upon his country's ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne treats ambition as a single dominating vice that can transform otherwise admirable traits into destructive behaviour; cautionary example: prefer avoiding the erection of personal glory at public expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard of extraordinary clemency depending on actor's fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Generous measures that work for Caesar are 'extraordinary means' that 'only appertain to Caesar's fortune,' and are not safe templates for ordinary leaders in civil war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Montaigne's warning that exemplary acts of clemency are context-dependent; they succeeded for Caesar because of his particular grandeur and fortune, not because they are universally advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation (use) is often more difficult and more virtuous than abstinence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Moderation is a virtue that gives more work than suffering; the well living of Scipio has a thousand fashions, that of Diogenes but one.' It is often harder to use gifts rightly than to renounce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne values reasoned use and regulation of appetites over extreme abstinence; prudence and regularity with one's gifts are preferable to self-mutilation or extreme renunciation (example: Spurina disfiguring himself is conscientious but 'defective in prudence').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit occasions and time: the captain's duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief part of a captain's skill is 'to know how to make use of occasions' and to be diligent in exploiting opportunities and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Caesar delayed an immediate answer to the Swiss envoys to use the time to gather his army. Guidance: use respites and seeming civility tactically to prepare your forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deception about enemy strength to maintain preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar, upon alarming reports of enemy forces, told his soldiers a number that 'much surpass[ed] both the truth and the report' so that finding an enemy weaker than expected is less dangerous than finding him stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He deliberately amplified enemy strength to avoid complacency; Montaigne cites Cyrus in Xenophon to justify prudent deception as preferable to underestimating a real threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational secrecy and unpredictability in issuing orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar accustoms soldiers simply to obey and communicates designs only at the point of execution; if soldiers discover intentions, he would change his orders to deceive them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep plans tightly held to preserve surprise; alter visible dispositions (e.g., lengthen march) to mislead observers and maintain strategic advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize valour; limit punishable faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar 'required no other virtue in a soldier but valour only' and seldom punished faults except mutiny and disobedience, sometimes dispensing soldiers from discipline after victories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motive: encourage ardour and loyalty. Anti-pattern: over-policing minor faults can demoralize; but unchecked licentiousness carries risks. Balance morale incentives with enforcement for serious infractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pomp, ornament, and honours as motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar loved to have soldiers richly armed and ornamented (engraved, gilded armour) so that 'the care of saving it might engage them to a more obstinate defence'; he called them 'fellow-soldiers' to flatter volunteers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige, visible rewards, and respectful forms of address can increase commitment. Note: Augustus later reformed the address to preserve imperial dignity — show tactics can be politically costly at higher levels of command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine courtesy with severity to command respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar mixed great courtesy with great severity: he used strict measures (e.g., cashiering a mutinous legion) to keep troops in awe while also employing kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective leadership can require both benevolence and decisive punishment; use severity sparingly but visibly to maintain authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal reconnaissance and presence: never quarter without viewing
rubrics_metrics.description: In enterprises of consequence Caesar 'always reconnoitred in person, and never brought his army into quarters till he had first viewed the place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should personally inspect terrain and conditions before settling forces; Montaigne notes Caesar even 'sounded the passage' when resolving to cross into England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value strategic counsel and patience over rash force
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar 'valued a victory obtained by counsel than by force' and sometimes declined an immediate advantage for a safer, later success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise temperance in taking risks; prefer a better-timed, less hazardous victory to a rash exploit that might squander hard-won glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor practical soldiering skills (swimming, marching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar believed swimming and marching on foot were of great use in war and personally practiced them (e.g., swimming to his fleet holding tablets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, physical competencies matter for commanders and soldiers alike; cultivate and exemplify basic martial skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer quality and manageability over sheer numbers in armies
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne endorses the proverb from Xenophon: 'Tis not the number of men, but the number of good men, that gives the advantage'; monstrous numbers often produce confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scanderbeg's view that 10–12 thousand reliable troops suffice; Bajazet's overreliance on numbers led to miscalculation. Aim for a moderate, well-provided, and governable force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shutting yourself up in a city unless last extremity
rubrics_metrics.description: A commander with responsibility for a whole country 'ought never to shut himself up' except when no other hope remains; he should keep freedom to provide for all parts of his government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain mobility and the ability to govern broadly; entrenchment in a fortress or city should be last resort as it surrenders strategic initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness, rapid movement, and logistical promptitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar's promptitude (e.g., rapid marches, quick returns) and ability to move forces swiftly were repeatedly decisive in his campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed and logistics can create strategic surprise and recover broad advantages; leaders should cultivate rapid mobilization and movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate soldier fidelity and mutual support
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesar's soldiers showed intense fidelity (offering to find men-at-arms at their own charge, defraying pay), and instances of besieged garrisons performing desperate sorties show high morale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster conditions that encourage mutual sacrifice and esprit de corps (shared costs, visible leadership, comradeship). Such loyalty can produce extraordinary feats but depends on passion and leadership as much as reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in marital affection: judge marriage by companionship conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The true touch and test of a happy marriage have respect to the time of the companionship, if it has been constantly gentle, loyal, and agreeable.' Public displays after death are poor evidence of true affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes ostentatious mourning and concealment of love during life — prefer consistent gentleness and loyalty over posthumous theatricality. He advises judging by behaviour during life (deportment, complexion, health) rather than formal lamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical mourning and prefer present affection
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They make the most ado who are least concerned' — excessive mourning after a husband's death often signals lack of genuine attachment during life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests not to be taken by bluster and ceremonial grief; genuine affection is shown by behaviour while the person lived. He also notes social motives (widow dressing for remarriage) as explanations for ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admirable but extreme examples of wifely loyalty and self-sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne records women (Pliny's neighbour, Arria, Pompeia Paulina) who advised or aided their husbands to death or even killed themselves to share their husbands' fate — acts presented as examples of 'austere' virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are extraordinary instances of devotion, admired for courage and loyalty; Montaigne selects them as rare models but notes that such extreme actions are not common and may be of a different order than ordinary virtue (hardly fit for imitation in everyday life).
